projectDesc.p: Encoded for the Experiencing War web site for the Veterans History Project.

samplingDecl.p: The recording of the interview with Dorothy Jeannette Mobley was digitized.

editorialDecl.p: This transcription was encoded with minimal changes to the original text in an effort to preserve original content and idiosyncrasies of the person interviewed. Period language and terminology are also retained. Encoding is literal with regard to the transcriptionist's capitalization, punctuation, and spelling. Spelling errors are indicated with [sic]; however, recurring errors in spelling within a single document have been marked the first time and not subsequently.

sp.speaker: Tony Regan
sp.p: It is May 17, 2002, we are at the Markoff (phonetic) Junior/Senior High School. We're interviewing Dorothy Mobley and Tony Regan and Stephanie Ward are going to be interviewing. And what type of work did you do when you were in the Army or Navy?

sp.speaker: Dorothy Jeannette Mobley
sp.p: I suppose it is wartime service. Well, I was a general mechanic helper.

sp.speaker: Tony Regan
sp.p: Okay, we will start the interview. We need to know your name.

sp.speaker: Dorothy Jeannette Mobley
sp.p: Dorothy J. Mobley.

sp.speaker: Tony Regan
sp.p: What was your maiden name?

sp.speaker: Dorothy Jeannette Mobley
sp.p: Dorothy Gray.

sp.speaker: Tony Regan
sp.p: And how old are you?

sp.speaker: Tony Regan
sp.p: Where were you born and raised?

sp.speaker: Dorothy Jeannette Mobley
sp.p: I was born about eight miles from Warcroft (phonetic).

sp.speaker: Tony Regan
sp.p: Okay, what was your family background?

sp.speaker: Dorothy Jeannette Mobley
sp.p: I had two brothers; both of them were in the service, in the Navy.

sp.speaker: Tony Regan
sp.p: Okay, What's your educational background?

sp.speaker: Dorothy Jeannette Mobley
sp.p: I graduated from Rosette, Wyoming, the 12th grade, in 1942.

sp.speaker: Tony Regan
sp.p: What's your current occupation?

sp.speaker: Dorothy Jeannette Mobley
sp.p: Domestic engineer.

sp.speaker: Tony Regan
sp.p: And your current address?

sp.speaker: Dorothy Jeannette Mobley
sp.p: 400 North Décor (phonetic).

sp.speaker: Tony Regan
sp.p: At the time of the War, were you in a relationship, married, or single?

sp.speaker: Dorothy Jeannette Mobley
sp.p: I was single when it started.

sp.speaker: Tony Regan
sp.p: Okay, what's your spouse's name and wartime occupation?

sp.speaker: Dorothy Jeannette Mobley
sp.p: Jack Mobley. He was in the Service, Air Corps, Army encampment, Casper. That soldier uniform turns ya on.

sp.speaker: Tony Regan
sp.p: If married, when and where were you married? You're married, but where were you married?

sp.speaker: Dorothy Jeannette Mobley
sp.p: Oh, we were married in Gillette, Wyoming.

sp.speaker: Tony Regan
sp.p: Okay, did you have any children at any time during the War? Well, my oldest one was born during the War, after Jack had gone overseas. He was born the day he landed in Italy.

sp.speaker: Tony Regan
sp.p: Where did you live or work during the War?

sp.speaker: Dorothy Jeannette Mobley
sp.p: In Casper, Wyoming.

sp.speaker: Tony Regan
sp.p: You worked as a mechanical --

sp.speaker: Dorothy Jeannette Mobley
sp.p: As Rosie the Riveter.

sp.speaker: Tony Regan
sp.p: What was your main wartime activity?

sp.speaker: Dorothy Jeannette Mobley
sp.p: Repairing the airplanes, I guess. Q Why did you choose that activity?

sp.speaker: Dorothy Jeannette Mobley
sp.p: Well, this is when so many of the boys had gone to Service so they were going to train the women to be able take over the wartime activity, so they started a pilot program in Casper and they're all graduates.

sp.speaker: Tony Regan
sp.p: What kind of training were you given?

sp.speaker: Dorothy Jeannette Mobley
sp.p: I was a sheet metal worker. We went to the school that had welding and they had, what was it? Welding and sheet metal and a shop where you done metal work. different activities. You could take either one you wanted to but this seemed like___(inaudible).

sp.speaker: Tony Regan
sp.p: So did you learn how to weld?

sp.speaker: Dorothy Jeannette Mobley
sp.p: No, I didn't. I didn't choose that department. I just -

sp.speaker: Tony Regan
sp.p: What was your title?

sp.speaker: Dorothy Jeannette Mobley
sp.p: What was my title? I guess I was a general mechanic helper.

sp.speaker: Tony Regan
sp.p: What did you like and dislike about being a general mechanical worker.

sp.speaker: Dorothy Jeannette Mobley
sp.p: I liked it because it was probably my first paycheck and I thought that was great, getting $125 a month.

sp.speaker: Tony Regan
sp.p: What did you dislike about it?

sp.speaker: Dorothy Jeannette Mobley
sp.p: Nothing really.

sp.speaker: Tony Regan
sp.p: What special roles or conventions did you have to follow?

sp.speaker: Dorothy Jeannette Mobley
sp.p: None really. We were well supervised so we done what they said to do.

sp.speaker: Tony Regan
sp.p: Who did you work for?

sp.speaker: Dorothy Jeannette Mobley
sp.p: Well, it was -- it would have been --it was at the Casper Air Base and I suppose that's what they'd say, the Army Airforce at the Sub Depot.

sp.speaker: Tony Regan
sp.p: Were you un-I-onized?

sp.speaker: Dorothy Jeannette Mobley
sp.p: You mean unionized?

sp.speaker: Tony Regan
sp.p: Yes.

sp.speaker: Dorothy Jeannette Mobley
sp.p: No we weren't in a union; you didn't have to belong to a union.

sp.speaker: Tony Regan
sp.p: Okay, did you develop friendships during the training or the activity itself?

sp.speaker: Dorothy Jeannette Mobley
sp.p: Oh yes, I had a lot of friends; I used to keep in contact with all of them, but kind of lost contact with a lot of them now. A lot of them passed away.

sp.speaker: Tony Regan
sp.p: How did you feel about the War?

sp.speaker: Dorothy Jeannette Mobley
sp.p: Well, I was too young to really think too much. I was just going with the flow then.

sp.speaker: Tony Regan
sp.p: How do you feel about it now?

sp.speaker: Dorothy Jeannette Mobley
sp.p: Well, I think it was something that had to be done. I think we done our job.

sp.speaker: Tony Regan
sp.p: And what ways did the war change your activities or habits?

sp.speaker: Dorothy Jeannette Mobley
sp.p: What days?

sp.speaker: Tony Regan
sp.p: What ways did the war change your activities or habits?

sp.speaker: Dorothy Jeannette Mobley
sp.p: Changed my life. I got married, went to North Carolina, had three boys; that really changed it.

sp.speaker: Tony Regan
sp.p: Sounds like it. What were some of the first changes in your life after the war started?

sp.speaker: Dorothy Jeannette Mobley
sp.p: What were some of the first changes? Well, I learned to be a housewife.

sp.speaker: Tony Regan
sp.p: What different responsibilities did you have to take on?

sp.speaker: Dorothy Jeannette Mobley
sp.p: With this?

sp.speaker: Tony Regan
sp.p: Yes.

sp.speaker: Dorothy Jeannette Mobley
sp.p: Well, what was the responsibilities we had to take on. Well, we had to just learn how to do these things and then after we'd had six weeks of training at the CNYA school and then we had to work at the air base.; we had to be there just like a job, you know. You were picked up, you went to work, you worked eight hours and then you went home. And it was shift work. You worked one of the three shifts.

sp.speaker: Tony Regan
sp.p: What time did usually work start for you?

sp.speaker: Dorothy Jeannette Mobley
sp.p: Well, you worked eight to four, then from four to midnight, then midnight to eight.

sp.speaker: Tony Regan
sp.p: How did you entertain yourself outside of work?

sp.speaker: Dorothy Jeannette Mobley
sp.p: Well, we had picture shows - that's about all -- the main entertainment there, and then ____(inaudible). About twice a month we had this counselor ,I guess you'd call her. Anyway, we'd have to entertain the soldiers at the USO.

sp.speaker: Dorothy Jeannette Mobley
sp.p: No, just dance.

sp.speaker: Tony Regan
sp.p: Did you worry whether our side would win, the United States?

sp.speaker: Dorothy Jeannette Mobley
sp.p: I don't think I was worried too much about it then.

sp.speaker: Tony Regan
sp.p: Did you know anyone who was killed or wounded in the war?

sp.speaker: Dorothy Jeannette Mobley
sp.p: Well, one of the boys we went to school with and took this training with, he got killed. That's about it. That's about all I know that got killed. That was shortly after he went overseas he got killed. He was in the Navy.

sp.speaker: Tony Regan
sp.p: What effect did the war have on your physical or mental health?

sp.speaker: Dorothy Jeannette Mobley
sp.p: None really; just got a husband.

sp.speaker: Tony Regan
sp.p: Do you think that medical care changed because of the war?

sp.speaker: Tony Regan
sp.p: Medical care?

sp.speaker: Dorothy Jeannette Mobley
sp.p: Uhhum. I really don't know whether I think it did or not. I suppose it did because of a lot of the war-related accidents and things.

sp.speaker: Tony Regan
sp.p: Was it Red Cross?

sp.speaker: Dorothy Jeannette Mobley
sp.p: Red Cross was really active during that time. In fact, my husband was going overseas when our baby was born, so we let the Red Cross know and then they let him know.

sp.speaker: Tony Regan
sp.p: Did you have worthwhile experiences because of the war?

sp.speaker: Dorothy Jeannette Mobley
sp.p: What?

sp.speaker: Tony Regan
sp.p: Did you have worthwhile experiences because of the war?

sp.speaker: Dorothy Jeannette Mobley
sp.p: A lot of letters I wrote every day.

sp.speaker: Tony Regan
sp.p: What was your most memorable experience?

sp.speaker: Dorothy Jeannette Mobley
sp.p: With?

sp.speaker: Tony Regan
sp.p: Anytime during those --

sp.speaker: Dorothy Jeannette Mobley
sp.p: During those times, during that -- most memorable experience. Well, I guess I could always remember, because I was smaller than most of the girls there, I always had to get up in the airplane wings -- they had what they call the bucking bar -- put these rivets in and put it up -- they would go up there and the rivet girl would go up there, rivet it up, put the gun on it and shoot it and then you'd have to sit on this side of the bucking bar and flatten it out to hold it, keep the metal on that you put on it.

sp.speaker: Tony Regan
sp.p: So you'd have to climb inside the wing?

sp.speaker: Dorothy Jeannette Mobley
sp.p: Uh hum. You know, with all these cross members and things around in there, you had to get up in there; if there's a hole in it you'd have to repair it.

sp.speaker: Tony Regan
sp.p: What kind of planes did you work on?

sp.speaker: Dorothy Jeannette Mobley
sp.p: B24s, B17s.

sp.speaker: Tony Regan
sp.p: Have you visited any memorials or participated in any com-memor-? I can't say that word.

sp.speaker: Dorothy Jeannette Mobley
sp.p: Commemorations?

sp.speaker: Tony Regan
sp.p: Yeah.

sp.speaker: Dorothy Jeannette Mobley
sp.p: Uh, no, we went to the 50th anniversary of the Casper Airbase, but that's where I worked but it was for the soldiers more but we got to go see where I worked and --

sp.speaker: Tony Regan
sp.p: Was there a lack of social opportunities and friends because of the war?

sp.speaker: Dorothy Jeannette Mobley
sp.p: No, I don't think there was.

sp.speaker: Tony Regan
sp.p: How did your community respond to the war and some of the differences?

sp.speaker: Dorothy Jeannette Mobley
sp.p: Our community was really active with publishing the papers and sending it to all these soldiers and letter writing. Of course I was gone most of the time then; I went to North Carolina and stayed there until he came back from overseas, at his home. Well, I came back here then after Jackie was six months old,.

sp.speaker: Tony Regan
sp.p: How did you cope with the wartime shortages?

sp.speaker: Dorothy Jeannette Mobley
sp.p: Well, we had a stamp for shoes, you had a little stamp for sugar and you got by; you didn't have about six pair of shoes and --

sp.speaker: Tony Regan
sp.p: The way it is now?

sp.speaker: Dorothy Jeannette Mobley
sp.p: Yeah, and you didn't -- you were real sure that you didn't had to use the sugar before you used it, you know. You didn't do a lot of cooking with desserts and things.

sp.speaker: Tony Regan
sp.p: What about recycling, like rubber, grease or other commodities? How did you guys recycle?

sp.speaker: Dorothy Jeannette Mobley
sp.p: Oh, during the war?

sp.speaker: Tony Regan
sp.p: Yeah.

sp.speaker: Dorothy Jeannette Mobley
sp.p: I don't remember recycling. I know we collected a lot of iron, anytime you needed iron, we'd have iron drives.

sp.speaker: Tony Regan
sp.p: How do you feel about war news from newsreels or radio?

sp.speaker: Dorothy Jeannette Mobley
sp.p: Now?

sp.speaker: Tony Regan
sp.p: Now and then?

sp.speaker: Dorothy Jeannette Mobley
sp.p: Well, I think we are pretty interested in it; you always look to see because anywhere where you were, had any relatives or something, you were kind of interested in what is doing.

sp.speaker: Tony Regan
sp.p: Do you remember when the war ended?

sp.speaker: Dorothy Jeannette Mobley
sp.p: Yes, I remember when the war ended.

sp.speaker: Tony Regan
sp.p: How did you feel?

sp.speaker: Dorothy Jeannette Mobley
sp.p: I was grateful.

sp.speaker: Tony Regan
sp.p: What's your most memorable time when the war ended? What do you remember most?

sp.speaker: Dorothy Jeannette Mobley
sp.p: Well, I just knew that Jack was stationed in South Carolina there; I just knew he would get to come home. So that was, you know.

sp.speaker: Tony Regan
sp.p: You must have been very excited? How would you describe the ways the war changed yours and the others' lives?

sp.speaker: Dorothy Jeannette Mobley
sp.p: How would I explain it? It made a change; things were much different after World War II than they were before. I don't know how but just offhand I can't think of --

sp.speaker: Tony Regan
sp.p: Did you keep your job or continue working after the war was over?

sp.speaker: Dorothy Jeannette Mobley
sp.p: With this job, no. When Jack got home, so -- I only worked there a little over a year, just worked at the airbase a little over a year.

sp.speaker: Tony Regan
sp.p: And you said you got paid a hundred and twenty --

sp.speaker: Dorothy Jeannette Mobley
sp.p: Yeah, a hundred and twenty-five dollars when I started and then I got a raise, and I was getting, I think it was a hundred and thirty-five dollars.

sp.speaker: Tony Regan
sp.p: Was that a lot of money back then?

sp.speaker: Dorothy Jeannette Mobley
sp.p: Boy that was a lot of money. Of course, you could only buy one pair of shoes, you know, every six months or something, so.

sp.speaker: Tony Regan
sp.p: I would die. (Laughter)

sp.speaker: Dorothy Jeannette Mobley
sp.p: Clothes, we always had a lot of clothes, we thought. But they didn't cost too much then. We lived right close to kind of an outlet store, I guess you'd call it now, so we did a lot of shopping there.

sp.speaker: Tony Regan
sp.p: Is there one thought about your wartime experience that you'd like to share with the future generations?

sp.speaker: Dorothy Jeannette Mobley
sp.p: Well, I didn't have much wartime experiences

sp.speaker: Tony Regan
sp.p: Or any experiences?

sp.speaker: Dorothy Jeannette Mobley
sp.p: Well, things are so much different than when they were doing that that, I don't know how to explain to anybody how to do things now. Just take advantage of it.

sp.speaker: Tony Regan
sp.p: Okay, Is there anything else that you'd like to add?

sp.speaker: Dorothy Jeannette Mobley
sp.p: Not that I know of.

sp.speaker: Tony Regan
sp.p: Thank you for your time. I think we can stop this now. (End of tape)
